title: Burst Quantization Orchestrator and Isolation Playbook (PRD Draft)
content:
Purpose:

This is a working PRD for a feature set we’re calling the Burst Quantization Orchestrator (BQO). The core idea: when customer workloads spike and Dedicated pools are under pressure, we should expand safe burst capacity not just by adding raw GPU slots but by temporarily switching eligible requests to quantized model paths and degraded QoS lanes that preserve latency SLOs while reducing cost and memory pressure.

Why this is different / motivation:
- Current burst plans rely on adding capacity or soft-evicting lower-priority tenants. That is expensive and brittle for on-prem/dedicated customers with fixed hardware.
- Quantization can reduce memory footprint and inference costs materially but has been applied globally per-model; we propose applying it dynamically per-request during bursts with tenant-aware controls and auditability.
- Combining smart request routing + short-lived quantization profiles + tenant isolation policies yields a gentler, lower-cost burst fabric that degrades output quality in a controlled, observable way.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Reduce peak GPU memory pressure during 90th/99th percentile bursts by ~30% for experimental workloads using BQO.
- Maintain 95th percentile tail latency SLOs for high-priority tenants during bursts via fast-failover to quantized lanes.
- Provide explicit tenant-level opt-in/opt-out controls plus per-tenant degradation budgets and audit logs.
- Expose simple knobs for Ops: burst threshold, quantization aggressiveness, per-tenant guardrails, and automatic rollback rules.

Non-goals:
- Not replacing full model-quantization onboarding for all models (that remains a separate Optimize surface).
- Not a permanent SLA change; BQO is for short-lived emergency/overflow windows.

Scope / users affected:
- Primary users: Platform and Product engineers, SRE/ops, account teams who manage Dedicated customers.
- Secondary: ML engineers who own models (we will need their signoff for safe quantization profiles).

High-level design:
1) Detection & Triggering
   - Metrics: GPU mem pressure, queue length, latency spikes, pool saturation.
   - Triggers: configurable thresholds (per-pool); multiple trigger modes (conservative, balanced, aggressive).
   - Safety: require 2 out of 3 signals to avoid flapping (mem pressure + queue length OR mem pressure + tail latency).

2) Quantization Profiles (Q-profiles)
   - Per-model small YAML describing compatible quantized variants: e.g., fp16->int8(prefers slower but smaller), mixed-int8, kv-cache-optimized int8.
   - Profiles include: expected memory reduction %, expected quality delta (estimated metrics), supported batch sizes, and fallthrough variant if inference fails.
   - Only models with precomputed Q-profiles (tested by Applied ML) are eligible. Ops can request new Q-profiles via a lightweight onboarding ticket.

3) Runtime Orchestration
   - Router consults policy engine: tenant priority, tenant degradation budget, region/pool, model eligibility.
   - Eligible requests are stamped for quantized execution; router may rewrite model->variant mapping and forward to a quantized pool or the same pool if runtime supports dual-path.
   - Fallback: If quantized path fails (OOM, kernel error, unacceptable latency), request is retried on a fallback lane (either original float model or a lower-priority queue) depending on tenant policy.

4) Isolation & Degradation Budgets
   - Per-tenant degradation budget: e.g., 5 minutes of quantized execution per 24h window or X tokens/day. Budgets replenish slowly and are configurable by account teams.
   - Soft isolation fence: tenants can opt into a shared burst fabric that accepts best-effort quantized bursts; others remain on strict lanes.
   - Emergency quiesce: in severe overload, non-critical tenants in the burst fabric can be rate-limited to preserve high-priority SLOs.

5) Observability & Auditing
   - Events: trigger start/stop, percent of traffic routed to quantized lanes, per-tenant budget usage, model quality regressions (if we have eval hooks).
   - Dashboards: per-pool burst dashboard, per-tenant degradation ledger, latency/cost delta panels.
   - Traceability: each quantized-executed response must carry metadata (Q-profile id, budget token id, fallback flag).

6) Operator Controls / Console UX
   - Single toggle to enable BQO per-dedicated-pool (default off).
   - Policy editor: fraction of traffic to consider, aggressiveness, tenant allowlist/blocklist, and manual evict/rollover actions.
   - Runbook actions: manual trigger, force-fallback, rebuild Q-profile.

Integration with Autoscaler & Existing Burst Mechanisms:
- Autoscaler remains primary for horizontal capacity; BQO is a complementary soft-burst mechanism for constrained environments or when scale cannot be provisioned quickly.
- When autoscaler adds nodes, BQO will ramp down; conversely, BQO can be a temporary stopgap while autoscale warmups complete.
- Important: handoff semantics — when autoscaler finishes, ensure in-flight quantized requests complete and new requests are sent to preferred float variant.

Operational runbook (surge example):
- Alert fires: "GPU mem pressure > 85% AND queue depth > 500".
- Ops checks dashboard: if BQO disabled, consider turning on in conservative mode for 10m.
- Watch degradation ledger: ensure top-tier customer X is not exceeding budget; temporarily whitelist if needed.
- If quantized path increases rejection or error rate above threshold, rollback immediately.
- Post-incident: run quality regressions for models that saw >10% traffic on Q-profiles and capture prompt-level examples for ML team.

Telemetry & SLOs to track:
- Percent traffic diverted to quantized lanes (per-pool, per-tenant).
- Tail latency delta for high-priority tenants during BQO windows.
- Quality regression signal: automated eval pass rate on a small prompt corpus sampled live.
- Budget exhaustion events and number of forced fallbacks.

Security / Compliance considerations:
- Audit logs for any tenant that experiences quantized execution (for regulated customers).
- Allow account-level opt-out for customers who must guarantee bit-exact or non-quantized outputs (finance/legal requirements).

Risks and mitigations:
- Quality regressions: mitigate with conservative default Q-profiles and strict per-tenant budgets; require ML signoff for model eligibility.
- Complexity/ops burden: provide clear console defaults and an automatic rollback on error spike.
- Poorly tuned profiles causing tail latency: require performance characterization (p95/p99) for each Q-profile before enabling.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default budget quota per tenant? token-based vs time-based? (Proposal: tokens keyed to total tokens processed on quantized path).
- Billing model: should we charge less for quantized-executed tokens? (ops likes the idea; finance wants clear invoicing).
- Should we support per-request opt-in via API flags (allowing customers to delegate control to SDKs)?

Next steps (concrete):
- Design spike: prototype router rewrite to map model->Q-variant (owner: eng-serving-runtime) — 2 weeks.
- Applied ML: generate Q-profiles for top 20 models used in Dedicated pools and publish expected deltas — 3 weeks.
- Console: add pool-level toggle and budget view (prod-dash) — 2 sprints.
- Pilot: pick 3 willing customers for a controlled pilot after Q-profile signoff.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a hybrid of autoscale and optimization approaches. Looking for feedback on tenant budget semantics and whether billing should reflect degraded execution. Also need confirmation from legal on audit log retention requirements.

-- end draft --
